Ever had a CDC pipeline that looked fine on the dashboard,
but you later discover missing records.

I just read about a nasty Debezium PostgreSQL failover edge case.
Everything seemed healthy after the failover,
PostgreSQL was up,
Debezium was running,
and there were no obvious errors.

The problem is that the replication slot on the new primary can start ahead of the offset Kafka Connect had stored.
That means the CDC stream looks healthy while events silently disappear.
I ran into a similar situation when a switchover happened during a batch load.
My monitoring missed the gap because the connector reported no lag.

Here are a few practical steps you can take:

- Persist the last processed LSN outside of Kafka Connect and compare it after a failover.
- Enable slot monitoring alerts for any backward movement in the offset.
- Run a checksum or row count comparison between source tables and the downstream sink after each topology change.

What safeguards have you added to detect silent CDC gaps?

#Debezium #PostgreSQL #CDC #DataEngineering

Ever wonder how a single platform can reshape our data pipelines?
Databricks just announced Lakebase and it feels like a new chapter for data engineering.
The idea is simple – combine the reliability of a data lake with the performance of a warehouse,
all in one unified layer.
From my experience,
having a single source of truth reduces the time spent on data movement and schema drift.
Here’s what I’m taking away from the announcement:
- You can run batch and streaming jobs side by side without juggling separate clusters.
- Governance becomes easier because metadata lives in one place.
- Cost predictability improves as you pay for compute only when you need it.
I’ve already started testing Lakebase on a small Spark job and the latency drop was noticeable.
If you’re building AI models,
the tighter integration with ML runtimes could shave days off feature engineering.
What do you think – is Lakebase the answer to our fragmented data stacks?
#DataEngineering #Lakebase #Databricks #AI
